```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(pwr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

set.seed(2025)  # every number in this report is reproducible
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Question

An A/B test compares the conversion rate of a control page (A) with a new variant (B). Suppose the true rates are **50% for A and 65% for B**. How many users does the test need to reliably detect that 15-point lift, and what goes wrong when it runs with too few?

All data here is **simulated**, so the true effect is known and we can check how often a test finds it.

## Step 1: Design the test before collecting data

Power is a property of the **design**: it is computed before any data exists, from the effect we assume (or the smallest effect we care about), the significance level and the sample size. Plugging the effect *observed* in the data back into a power formula ("observed" or "post-hoc" power) is a known fallacy: it is a one-to-one function of the p-value and adds no information. So every power value in this report uses the assumed true effect.

Cohen's *h* puts the difference between two proportions on a common scale (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large).

```{r design}
alpha <- 0.05
p_A <- 0.50
p_B <- 0.65
h <- ES.h(p_B, p_A)

# Planned small test: 50 users in total, 25 per group
n_small_per_group <- 25
power_small <- pwr.2p.test(h = h, n = n_small_per_group, sig.level = alpha)$power

# Sample size for 80% power. pwr.2p.test returns n PER GROUP; round up.
design_80 <- pwr.2p.test(h = h, power = 0.80, sig.level = alpha)
n_large_per_group <- ceiling(design_80$n)

data.frame(
  quantity = c("Cohen's h", "Power with 25 per group",
               "n per group for 80% power (exact)", "n per group (rounded up)", "Total users"),
  value = c(round(h, 3), round(power_small, 3), round(design_80$n, 1),
            n_large_per_group, 2 * n_large_per_group)
) %>% kable()
```

With 25 users per group the test has only about a **`r round(100 * power_small)`% chance** of detecting a real 15-point lift. Reaching 80% power needs **`r n_large_per_group` per group (`r 2 * n_large_per_group` in total)**.

## Step 2: Check the power formula by simulation

`pwr` uses a normal approximation. To check it, we simulate many experiments at each sample size, analyse each with the same two-proportion test (`prop.test`, no continuity correction), and record how often p < 0.05. That share *is* the power.

```{r monte-carlo}
n_sims <- 2000
sim_once <- function(n) {
  x <- c(rbinom(1, n, p_A), rbinom(1, n, p_B))
  test <- prop.test(x, c(n, n), correct = FALSE)
  c(p = test$p.value, diff = (x[2] - x[1]) / n)
}

grid <- c(10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 170, 225, 300)
mc <- lapply(grid, function(n) {
  r <- replicate(n_sims, sim_once(n))
  data.frame(n_per_group = n, p = r["p", ], diff = r["diff", ])
}) %>% bind_rows()

mc_power <- mc %>%
  group_by(n_per_group) %>%
  summarise(simulated_power = mean(p < alpha), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(analytic_power = sapply(n_per_group, function(n)
           pwr.2p.test(h = h, n = n, sig.level = alpha)$power))

kable(mc_power, digits = 3,
      caption = "Power: pwr formula vs share of 2,000 simulated tests with p < 0.05")
```

```{r power-curve}
curve_df <- data.frame(n_per_group = 5:320) %>%
  mutate(power = sapply(n_per_group, function(n)
           pwr.2p.test(h = h, n = n, sig.level = alpha)$power))

p_curve <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(n_per_group, power)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0073C2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = mc_power, aes(y = simulated_power), size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(n_small_per_group, n_large_per_group),
             linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = n_small_per_group + 5, y = 0.05, hjust = 0,
           label = sprintf("25/group: %.0f%%", 100 * power_small)) +
  annotate("text", x = n_large_per_group + 5, y = 0.6, hjust = 0,
           label = sprintf("%d/group: 80%%", n_large_per_group)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Power to detect 50% vs 65% conversion",
       subtitle = "Line: pwr formula. Points: 2,000 simulated tests each",
       x = "Users per group", y = "Power") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
p_curve
ggsave("figures/power_curve.png", p_curve, width = 7, height = 4.2, dpi = 120)
```

The simulated points sit on the analytic curve, so the formula can be trusted for planning at these sample sizes.

## Step 3: One experiment at each sample size

This is what a single team would actually see. We report the estimated lift with a 95% confidence interval, not just the p-value.

```{r single-runs}
run_experiment <- function(n_per_group, label) {
  conv <- data.frame(
    group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = n_per_group),
    conversion = c(rbinom(n_per_group, 1, p_A), rbinom(n_per_group, 1, p_B))
  )
  x <- tapply(conv$conversion, conv$group, sum)
  test <- prop.test(x[c("B", "A")], c(n_per_group, n_per_group), correct = FALSE)
  list(
    data = mutate(conv, design = label),
    row = data.frame(
      Design = label,
      Users_per_group = n_per_group,
      Conv_A = x[["A"]] / n_per_group,
      Conv_B = x[["B"]] / n_per_group,
      Lift_B_minus_A = unname(test$estimate[1] - test$estimate[2]),
      CI_low = test$conf.int[1],
      CI_high = test$conf.int[2],
      p_value = test$p.value,
      Planned_power = pwr.2p.test(h = h, n = n_per_group, sig.level = alpha)$power
    )
  )
}

small <- run_experiment(n_small_per_group, "Small (25/group)")
large <- run_experiment(n_large_per_group, sprintf("Powered (%d/group)", n_large_per_group))
summary_df <- bind_rows(small$row, large$row)
kable(summary_df, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "One simulated experiment per design (true lift = 0.15)")
```

```{r single-runs-plot}
plot_df <- bind_rows(small$data, large$data) %>%
  group_by(design, group) %>%
  summarise(x = sum(conversion), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(rate = x / n,
         lo = prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int[1],
         hi = prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int[2]) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(design = factor(design, levels = c(small$row$Design, large$row$Design)))

p_bars <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(group, rate, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), width = 0.15) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(p_A, p_B), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~ design) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#EFC000", B = "#0073C2"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Observed conversion with 95% Wilson intervals",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines: true rates (50% and 65%)",
       x = "Group", y = "Conversion rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
p_bars
ggsave("figures/conversion_by_design.png", p_bars, width = 7, height = 4.2, dpi = 120)
```

In this run the small test estimated a lift of `r round(small$row$Lift_B_minus_A, 2)`, but its 95% interval runs from `r round(small$row$CI_low, 2)` to `r round(small$row$CI_high, 2)` (p = `r round(small$row$p_value, 2)`). The powered test estimated `r round(large$row$Lift_B_minus_A, 2)` with an interval of `r round(large$row$CI_low, 2)` to `r round(large$row$CI_high, 2)` (p = `r signif(large$row$p_value, 2)`). The "Planned_power" column is the design power for the true effect, not something estimated from these data.

A single run is an anecdote: with this seed the outcomes are as shown, but another seed could give a significant small test or a non-significant powered one. Step 2 is the real evidence. Note also that a non-significant result in the small test would **not** show that A and B convert equally. Its confidence interval is wide enough to include both no effect and a large one; the test simply could not tell them apart.

## Step 4: The hidden cost of underpowered tests (winner's curse)

Underpowered tests miss real effects most of the time. They also mislead when they *do* reach significance: only the luckiest, most exaggerated estimates clear the bar.

```{r winners-curse}
curse <- mc %>%
  filter(n_per_group %in% c(10, 25, 170)) %>%
  group_by(n_per_group) %>%
  summarise(
    share_significant = mean(p < alpha),
    mean_lift_all = mean(diff),
    mean_lift_if_significant = mean(diff[p < alpha]),
    exaggeration_ratio = mean(abs(diff[p < alpha])) / (p_B - p_A),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
kable(curse, digits = 3,
      caption = "True lift is 0.15. Averages over 2,000 simulated tests per row.")
```

Across all runs the estimate is unbiased at every sample size. But among significant results only, small tests overstate the lift (exaggeration ratio well above 1), while at the planned `r n_large_per_group` per group the significant estimates are close to the truth.

## Conclusions

- **Plan the sample size first.** Detecting a 50% → 65% lift (Cohen's *h* = `r round(h, 2)`) with 80% power at α = 0.05 needs `r n_large_per_group` users per group. With 25 per group the power is only `r round(100 * power_small)`%.
- **The power formula holds up.** Simulated power matched `pwr.2p.test` across sample sizes.
- **Underpowered tests fail in two ways:** they usually miss a real effect (Type II error), and when they do hit significance, they exaggerate it.
- **Report intervals, not just p-values,** and never read "not significant" as "no difference".

## Limitations

- Simulated data with a known, fairly large effect (15 points). Real conversion lifts are usually much smaller, so real tests need far more users.
- One test, one metric. Testing several metrics or variants needs a multiple-comparison correction, and checking results repeatedly before the planned sample size ("peeking") inflates false positives. See the companion Python project.

Companion project: [ml-model-ab-test-framework](https://github.com/lukahere007/ml-model-ab-test-framework) applies this design-first workflow to comparing two ML models (accuracy and latency), with a tested Python implementation of the same sample size formula.
